en: When cold lake water touches Taal Volcano's hot magma, it instantly flashes into steam, causing massive explosive eruptions.
Mayon Volcano's perfect conical shape forms because its highly viscous lava cools quickly and piles up near the vent instead of flowing far.
The Pasig River temporarily reverses its flow direction when high tide in Manila Bay pushes seawater upstream against the river's current.
Dense mangrove forests in Palawan protect coastlines from storm surges because their tangled roots absorb wave energy and trap sediment.
The Tiwi geothermal power plant generates electricity by using underground volcanic heat to boil water into steam that spins turbines.
Philippine typhoons gain immense wind strength because they absorb heat energy and moisture from the warm tropical waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Corals in the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park lose their vibrant colors and starve when unusually warm ocean waters expel their symbiotic algae.
The Amihan season brings cool, dry weather to the Philippines because high-pressure systems in Asia push cold northeast winds across the country.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park formed over millions of years as slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the region's limestone bedrock.
The deep Philippine Trench forms because the Philippine Sea Plate is forced downward, or subducted, beneath the moving Eurasian Plate.
Deforestation in the Sierra Madre mountains increases severe flooding in nearby lowlands because bare soil cannot absorb heavy monsoon rainfall.
Bohol's Chocolate Hills turn brown during the dry season because the intense sun dries out the grass covering the limestone mounds.
